etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Old French conjonction, from Latin coniūnctiō (“joining”), from coniungere (“to join”).

definitions.definition: The act of joining, or condition of being joined.

quote.citation: 1871–1872, George Eliot [pseudonym; Mary Ann Evans], chapter XVIII, in Middlemarch […], volume (please specify |volume=I to IV), Edinburgh, London: William Blackwood and Sons, →OCLC, book I:
quote.text: […]  Dr. Minchin in return was quite sure that man was not a mere machine or a fortuitous conjunction of atoms;  […]

quote.citation: 1896, Robert Louis Stevenson, Familiar Studies of Men and Books‎[1]:
quote.text: About them all there is that sort of stiff quaint unreality, that conjunction of the grotesque, and even of a certain bourgeois snugness, with passionate contortion and horror, that is so characteristic of Gothic art.

definitions.definition: (grammar) A word used to join other words, phrases, or clauses together into sentences. (The specific conjunction used shows how the two joined parts are related semantically.)

quote.citation: 1881, Alfred Ayres [pseudonym; Thomas Embly Osmun], The Verbalist‎[2]:
quote.text: A comma is placed between short members of compound sentences, connected by and, but, for, nor, or, because, whereas, that expressing purpose (so that, in order that), and other conjunctions.

quote.citation: 1843, John Stuart Mill, A System of Logic‎[3], volume 1:
quote.text: […]  the coexistence of one such phenomenon with another; or the succession of one such phenomenon to another: their conjunction, in short, so that where the one is found, we may calculate on finding both.

definitions.definition: (astronomy) The alignment of two bodies in the solar system such that they have the same longitude when seen from Earth.

quote.text: The spectacular conjunction of Venus and Mars gave rise to a myriad of mythical interpretations.

definitions.definition: (astrology) An aspect in which planets are in close proximity to one another.
A place where multiple things meet.

quote.citation: 2001, David L. Lieber, Jules Harlow, Etz Hayim: Torah and Commentary, page 47:
quote.text: Today there is a mountain called Ararat near the conjunction of the Turkish, Armenian, and Iranian borders.

quote.citation: 1603, Michel de Montaigne, chapter 29, in John Florio, transl., The Essayes […], book I, London:  […]  Val[entine] Simmes for Edward Blount […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Certaine Nations (and amongst others, the Mahometane) abhorre Conjunction with women great with childe.
